resident.chief_complaint: Bilateral upper and lower limb weakness and inability to walk for 4 months, gradually progressive.
resident.history: The patient was apparently healthy 4 months prior. Over 4 months, he developed bilateral upper and lower limb weakness and inability to walk, which was gradually progressive. There was no history of trauma, fever, weight loss, or loss of appetite. Bowel and bladder function were spared. No dysphagia or difficulty breathing.
resident.physical_exam: Muscle power in both upper and lower limbs was 3/5. Bilateral Hoffman's sign was positive. All reflexes were exaggerated. There was difficulty in tandem gait. Clonus was absent. Bowel and bladder were spared.
key_positive_signs: Bilateral upper and lower limb weakness with muscle power 3/5
Multiple contiguous ossifications of anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments from C2 to T1 and thoracic/lumbar spine
OPLL with multiple level cord compression at cervical spine
resident.past_history: The patient was apparently healthy 4 months ago. No other past medical history is documented.
resident.public_message: This is a 69-year-old male who presented with bilateral upper and lower limb weakness and inability to walk for 4 months, gradually progressive. He was apparently healthy 4 months earlier, with no trauma, fever, weight loss, or loss of appetite. Bowel and bladder function was spared, and there was no dysphagia or breathing difficulty. Physical examination showed muscle power 3/5 in all limbs, bilateral Hoffman's sign positive, exaggerated reflexes, difficulty with tandem gait, and no clonus. Radiological examination demonstrated multiple contiguous ossifications of the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments from C2 to T1 and in the thoracic and lumbar spine, with normal sacroiliac joints; there was cervical OPLL with multilevel cord compression. No separate laboratory data are available.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record’s description only; the films were not available for review. The record describes multilevel cervical cord compression associated with ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament from C2 through T1, with the dominant abnormality being multilevel cervical involvement. Stenosis severity and cord T2 signal are not stated in the record.

neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord, likely multilevel (C2–T1), consistent with myelopathy from ventral compression due to OPLL. Bilateral upper and lower limb weakness with hyperreflexia and Hoffman's sign localizes above C5 and below the brainstem; absence of bulbar signs supports cervical rather than brainstem localization. Bowel and bladder sparing is consistent with early or partial cord involvement.

red_flags.finding: Thoracolumbar ossifications of the posterior longitudinal ligament are described, but thoracic/lumbar cord compression is not documented.
red_flags.rationale: The dominant syndrome is explained by cervical cord compression; lower limb signs are already attributable to the cervical lesion. Without documented thoracic cord compression or T2 signal change, this does not change the indication or plan, but it is a coexisting finding that may warrant attention if surgical planning extends beyond the cervical spine.

neurology.public_message: Localization is to the cervical spinal cord, with multilevel ventral compression from OPLL explaining the bilateral pyramidal weakness and Hoffman's sign. The match between symptoms and imaging is high; the dominant syndrome of progressive myelopathy is well explained by the documented multilevel cervical cord compression. One coexisting red flag is noted: thoracolumbar ossifications are present but without documented cord compression, so they do not alter the cervical localization or current indication; they should be kept in mind if the surgical plan extends caudally. The examination as documented lacks sensory, cranial nerve, and detailed reflex grading, so localization rests on an incomplete examination. No symptom-imaging mismatch is identified.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA physical status III. Intraoperative mean arterial pressure target 80 mmHg. Blood loss risk moderate. Extubation difficulty unassessable because no airway assessment is documented. Prone position tolerance low.

preconditions_for_failure: Neurological deterioration during conservative treatment (decline in motor power, new long-tract signs, or sphincter dysfunction)
No meaningful functional improvement in ambulation or activities of daily living after 3 months of supervised rehabilitation
MRI evidence of cord signal change (T2 hyperintensity) or increase in cord compression on follow-up imaging
Development of severe pain or instability that precludes participation in rehabilitation
physiatrist_opening.public_message: I recommend a structured conservative program for 3-6 months. Although the progressive nature of this myelopathy is concerning and evidence suggests surgery may be more effective for severe cases, a trial of intensive rehabilitation remains a reasonable option in selected patients without rapid deterioration or sphincter involvement. The program should include physical therapy for gait and balance, core stabilization, cervical isometric strengthening, posture education, fall prevention, and pain management. Conservative treatment would be considered failed if there is further neurological decline, no functional improvement after 3 months, or new bowel/bladder symptoms. We should obtain serial MRI to assess cord signal; if cord T2 hyperintensity is present or myelopathy progresses, surgical referral should be expedited.

physiatrist_final.public_message: The surgical argument points to progressive myelopathy and extensive OPLL, both of which are already central to my risk assessment and were explicitly acknowledged in my opening. The record does not document rapid deterioration, sphincter involvement, or cord T2 signal change; bowel and bladder are spared, and no clonus is noted. Multilevel ossification alone, even extensive, does not by itself make a three-to-six-month supervised rehabilitation trial unsafe when failure criteria and serial MRI surveillance are in place. I therefore hold to conservative management for now, with expedited surgical referral if any of the stated failure criteria emerge.

vice_opinions.assessment: This is a 69-year-old male with progressive cervical myelopathy over 4 months, now non-ambulatory with 3/5 strength in all limbs and upper motor neuron signs. Imaging documents extensive ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament from C2 to T1 with multilevel cord compression. The clinical picture is consistent with severe, progressive myelopathy. Without surgical decompression, there is high risk of further irreversible neurological deterioration. Additional imaging (MRI with cord signal, CT for OPLL extent and dural ossification) and airway assessment are needed before final surgical planning.
proposed_options: Posterior cervical decompression and instrumented fusion (likely C2–T1 laminectomy with fusion) as primary surgical strategy for multilevel OPLL.
Cervical laminoplasty (C3–7 or extended) without fusion, preserving motion but less reliable for very extensive or kyphotic OPLL.
Anterior cervical corpectomy and fusion for focal anterior compression, though technically challenging and higher risk for this long-segment ossified lesion.
Combined anterior-posterior decompression and fusion if posterior-only decompression proves inadequate or if significant kyphosis or focal anterior compression is present.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior cervical decompression and instrumented fusion (extent to be determined by further imaging, likely C2–T1).
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatrist's recommendation for a 3–6 month conservative trial in this progressive, severe myelopathy with documented multilevel cord compression; standard spine practice favors early surgical decompression to prevent irreversible cord damage.

The optimal surgical approach for extensive OPLL (anterior vs posterior vs combined) remains debated; I favor posterior decompression but acknowledge that a subset of surgeons would argue for an anterior or staged approach depending on OPLL thickness and cord signal.
The absence of documented cord T2 signal, dural ossification, and detailed airway assessment limits final surgical planning; these must be obtained before a definitive approach is chosen.

Whether the thoracic and lumbar ossifications require any intervention is unsettled; I would defer addressing them unless they cause clinical symptoms or demonstrate significant cord compression on further imaging.
deferred_questions_to_director: Final decision on surgical approach and timing.
Whether to include C2 in the decompression/fusion and whether to extend across the cervicothoracic junction.
Whether any intervention is needed for the thoracic/lumbar OPLL in this setting.
Confirmation of the appropriate preoperative imaging and airway workup.
vice_opinions.public_message: Surgical decompression is indicated for this progressive cervical myelopathy due to extensive OPLL. I recommend posterior cervical decompression and instrumented fusion as the primary strategy, with further imaging and airway assessment prior to scheduling.

director_rulings.final_decision: Surgery is indicated. Proceed with posterior cervical decompression and instrumented fusion from C2 to T1. Preoperative MRI and CT will finalize the decompression details and confirm the need for any anterior supplementation: if OPLL occupies more than 50% of the canal or there is significant kyphosis, an anterior or combined approach will be considered. The thoracic and lumbar ossifications will not be addressed unless imaging shows significant cord compression or they become symptomatic. A conservative trial is rejected in this progressive, severe myelopathy.
director_rulings.surgical_plan: Posterior cervical decompression (laminectomy) with instrumented fusion C2–T1, including C2 if involved and extending to T2 if adjacent-level instability is demonstrated. Intraoperative neuromonitoring will be used. No intervention for thoracic/lumbar OPLL unless significant cord compression or symptoms are identified on further imaging.

I recommend a structured conservative program for 3-6 months. Although the progressive nature of this myelopathy is concerning and evidence suggests surgery may be more effective for severe cases, a trial of intensive rehabilitation remains a reasonable option in selected patients without rapid deterioration or sphincter involvement. The program should include physical therapy for gait and balance, core stabilization, cervical isometric strengthening, posture education, fall prevention, and pain management. We should obtain serial MRI to assess cord signal; if cord T2 hyperintensity is present or myelopathy progresses, surgical referral should be expedited.

Surgical decompression is indicated for this progressive cervical myelopathy due to extensive OPLL. I recommend posterior cervical decompression and instrumented fusion as the primary strategy, with further imaging and airway assessment prior to scheduling.

The surgical argument points to progressive myelopathy and extensive OPLL, both of which are already central to my risk assessment and were explicitly acknowledged in my opening.
